h.strategy: Naive reasoning predicts substitution: if something similar exists elsewhere, an edit helps less. Experts find this obvious, so at most two hypotheses may use it. At least three hypotheses must predict the opposite, complementarity, where an edit helps MORE because a different kind of component elsewhere supplies what it lacks. At least two must predict a reversal, where a usually beneficial edit becomes harmful under a specific condition through trainability, merged-signal scale, or over-capacity. Never condition on the edited field's own value or on settings that make the edit inert. Each hypothesis must couple two different fields, and no condition setting may appear more than twice. In each 'why', give the mechanism in two or three sentences, state why an expert might bet the other way, and name the refuting comparison. The critic should replace any hypothesis that duplicates another's mechanism.

hyps.why: Two parallel identity paths into node 3 are redundant, so the second skip adds less than it would beside a conv on edge 4.
Node 3 already has a strong direct 3x3 path, so a second 3x3 conv on edge 5 gives diminishing returns.
Replacing a removed edge with a 3x3 conv restores a learned path into node 3, a larger gain than upgrading an existing op.
A skip into node 3 helps most when other paths are weak, so its gain shrinks when edge 5 is already a strong conv.
Node 2 already receives a strong 3x3 conv from edge 1, so an added 1x1 on edge 2 saturates rather than complements.
With edge 0 removed, edge 1 is the only input-fed route into node 2, so a conv there matters far more.
With edge 0 removed, node 1 carries no signal so a conv on edge 2 has almost nothing to act on.
With edge 0 removed, node 1 is zero so edge 4 cannot contribute and the conv gain collapses.
Replacing a removed direct edge with a conv gains more than replacing an already useful op, since it restores the short input-to-output path.
Replacing a removed edge 0 re-activates node 1 and its two outgoing paths, a much larger gain than upgrading an existing op.
